This work presents the theoretical foundations and design rules for wideband waveforming that integrates data transmission with energy delivery across SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM frameworks. Although the underlying mathematics for Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) systems become intractably difficult, these complexities are avoided by adapting the methodology to two-dimensional designs involving multiple carriers but either single-send or multiple-receive capabilities. This shift fundamentally shifts the focus from resolving the constraints of WxW (waveforming dimension) challenges—which arise when both data transmission (D) and wireless power transfer (HWI) operate on full WIMO with multiple antennas—to addressing integrated D+HWI in WxS (wideband receive) or D+HWI in WxS configurations instead.

This work presents a new numerical technique for tracking material interfaces by integrating a level-set method with Cartesian embedded boundary techniques. This combination offers an efficient implementation while preserving the continuity of physical quantities across the boundary. The approach's implementation and properties are examined through a one-dimensional test, and its performance in two spatial dimensions is validated against results from a circular interface model. Finally, the method's practical utility is demonstrated by simulating various heat-driven convection scenarios, including Stefan-Boussinesq and partially melted configurations.

In contrast to the predominant existing methods for estimating equilibria in multi-player games, which often prioritize finding a solution with minimal support, this paper focuses on prioritizing explainability with respect to player strategies. We analyze both Shapley Value-based approaches and an innovative bottom-up game transformation method applied specifically to a class of games that demonstrate value stability. Our findings reveal that these simplified strategies inherently fail to provide convincing explanations for payoff structures, highlighting a clear constraint in current algorithms that primarily support minimal strategies. To investigate this limitation regarding strategy support versus explanatory power, we evaluate both the shapley value-based minimal supports and our proposed method on the newly constructed "TEB game." Additionally, we assess human performance when participants play versions of this game assuming a minimal strategy-based equilibrium. Results from both the TEB game assessment and subjective human studies indicate that while the shapley value-based minimal supports are ineffective at providing convincing justifications via payoff structures, our method is significantly more successful in achieving this ex post explanation goal.

This study analyzes a stochastic SIR (susceptible, infectious, recovered) epidemic model defined on a finite graph that evolves through a continuous-time process. This graph transformation occurs independently of the epidemic dynamics via a mechanism known as preventive rewiring, which triggers whenever an individual transitions from the infectious to the recovered state. This action temporarily isolates the individual's most recently infected neighbor—effectively removing the edge between them—for a set duration $\tau$ before the node and its edges are restored to the "susceptible" pool, with the total process terminating upon the graph becoming isolation. The paper first establishes that as the initial number of people, $N$, increases towards infinity (while $\tau$ and all related parameters stay constant), these dynamics converge strongly in distribution to those of a deterministic system of integral equations to fixed limits. Furthermore, the research examines the final size distribution of the outbreak under various conditions for $\tau$. It specifically highlights how the limit epidemic curve shifts as a function of the total population count and the timing duration $\tau$, discussing these findings within a broader context.

Achieving the most reliable values and uncertainty intervals for parton distribution function (PDF) parameters requires a theory framework that is explicitly integrated into global analyses of experimental and numerical data. While the modern Bayesian interpretation of PDF fitting has gained significant traction, it is by no means the sole required approach; a robust Bayesian setup demands prior distributions for both the PDF parameters and all confounding variables, regardless of whether these alternatives offer a fully consistent Bayesian solution. To address the latter rigorously, this paper introduces a novel theoretical Bayes factor formulation to quantify discrepancies between perturbative QCD evolution schemes, as well as updates from global analyses incorporating new datasets or theoretical advancements. Finally, we demonstrate and provide an operational code implementation for combining experimental data with such theoretical Bayes factors.

In the domain of collaborative reinforcement learning (CRL), the effective large-scale policy enhancement relies significantly on efficient sample utilization. This study introduces Variance-Diminution based Experience Replay (VDR), a batch sample optimization methodology designed to address this need. The core premise of VDR is that sample weights assigned within experience replay buffers should reflect the return distribution's variance, prioritizing more informative data while variances are reduced, fewer samples are selected. Our analysis demonstrates that VDR offers theoretical advantages, including asymptotic convergence guarantees and an integrated return variance that is strictly smaller than alternatives utilizing uniform sampling weights. To validate the efficacy of this method, extensive experiments were conducted using various standard reinforcement learning benchmarks alongside a real-world deployed scenario.

This investigation examines the interaction between a turbulent, methane-air jet flame and acoustic forcing within a linearized framework, employing the active flame model. This approach linearizes Schlichting's instability theory around a jet dispersion solution to anticipate flame dynamics under specific parameters and incoming disturbances, without requiring a specific configuration or individual forcing mechanism. To represent forcing in the current setup, the active flame model is modified to incorporate an arbitrary transfer function, with selections made to mimic a thermo-acoustic resonator. Utilizing these parameters, the model captures both primary fluctuations resulting from intrinsic jet instability and phase-lagged responses typical of resonators. Additionally, it depicts complex flame dynamics induced by forced inertial ranges and a noise-like response associated with intrinsic boundary layers of the jet. Finally, predicted velocity fields are compared against experimental data obtained by Kim et al., with outcomes showing strong agreement.

Nonlocal gravity constitutes a specific class of modified gravity theories where the divergence of the Einstein tensor relies solely on the curvature tensors. We demonstrate that by adopting an appropriate definition for local coupling, these theories reformat into a "derivative-coupled nonlocal gravity" framework, the sourced side of which features a well-defined effective Ricci tensor sourced by the standard Einstein tensor. We argue this effective Ricci tensor must satisfy specific stability criteria to forestall vacuum inconsistencies and logical contradictions arising from nonderivative couplings. Furthermore, we develop general constitutive equations for a multilinear, two-point operator-based source theory applicable to vacuum propagation scenarios. Finally, we linearize these relations to explore propagation modes in flat spacetime, listing various nonlocal vacuum propagation scenarios accordingly.

We propose a unified framework to enhance Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS) by integrating eight different functional genomics annotations. Our approach employs a linear model that incorporates an $N \times T$ matrix representing GWAS SNP-significance scores and a set of $N \times K$ matrices containing various functional genome annotations. Here, $N$ denotes the total number of SNPs, while $K$ denotes the number of functional annotations (T denotes transposition for convenience). Assuming these functional genomes operate as independent sources of information regarding SNP functionality, we determine the model's optimal parameters through a closed-form expression and derive enhanced association $Z$ scores using our derived SNP significance measures. Consequently, this process effectively reweighting SNP associations in accordance with genomic functionality to create an initial "functionalized" or "pre-ranked" list of associations. This pre-ranked list serves as optimized input for downstream genetic analysis methods, such as Fine-mapping, Fine-Map, Polygenic Risk Score (PRS), Summary-based Risk Ratio (sumBa), and Genetic Relatedness Matrix (grema). As a direct application, we fine-mapped associations across 18 human traits, including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), breast cancer (both general and Asian-specific), coronary artery disease, height, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), type 2 diabetes, and recent findings from genome-wide scans of Alzheimer's disease. Often treated as a static background, the crystal lattice is here recognized as an active participant in quantum dynamics. Specifically, we demonstrate that moving electrons generate both phonons and spin waves (magnons). This happens because object motion creates a relativistic effect that breaks inversion symmetry, generating a momentum-dependent, dynamic coupling between electrons and phonons, as well as between electrons and spin. We titled this phenomenon \textit{momentum-induced dynamic interactions}. Within the mean-field framework, this coupling yields a complex, momentum-displacement feedback loop driven by relativistic terms; furthermore, it produces a spin-phono-interactive feedback mechanism within the Hubbard model. Our approach involves deriving a general formalism for inverse transformations between inertial frames in quasicrystals to derive these interactions. We illustrate these concepts using specific models: a single-site Frenkel-Kramers-Ponds (FKP) coupling to the Holstein (H) model highlights how object movement generates phonons and creates complex feedback loops from the combined Holm and Heitler-Raise (HHR) models. Additionally, we show that mobility induces \textit{momentum-dependent e} and spin-electric (SE) coupling. Finally, we present numerical results based on HMR and SEM simulations.

Substellar objects with masses lower than that of degenerate stars can exist as either fluids in thermal equilibrium or in non-equilibrium states lacking degeneration. These bodies do not sustain rotational equilibrium through central degeneration; instead, they rely on a centrifugal balance between self-gravity and self-pressure at their surfaces or within non-coaxing magnetic fields. To examine how rotating non-degenerate thermal subsellar objects behave, we conducted simulations of rotation and hydrodynamic equilibrium for both self-magnetic field-stalled bodies (in total rotational equilibrium) and those trapped by magnetic fields (without rotational equilibrium). Our results demonstrate that thermally cool, non-degenerated bodies built from hydrogen can reach mass ejection limits via rotation. We further investigate the internal dynamics, temperature gradients, and structural characteristics of these astrophysical candidates, comparing them against observations from floating in space of mass ejection and magnetic fields to assess whether they align with known astronomical data. A more capable regulation strategy is proposed for multi-agent systems where each agent can perform several independent single-agent tasks. While similar strategies exist, most do not account for limitations in an agent's communication and computation. In this model, every agent is capable of executing multiple tasks using individual controllers, but faces constraints on how much they can compute and communicate. The goal of each agent is to minimize the combined cost of all assigned tasks. Smart wearable devices have significantly advanced the field of personal health, yet user data privacy and the limitations of traditional centralized models remain critical challenges. To address these issues and maximize the benefits of health monitoring, we introduce FedHealth—a federated transfer knowledge framework designed to evolve wearables-based healthcare applications. The core of our design lies in a transfer knowledge component that enrichens the initial federated learning process. Specifically, we utilize knowledge gained from a non-federated source to give the initial model a stronger baseline, enabling it to converge more quickly. Furthermore, during the subsequent federated learning phase, we incorporate an fine-tuning step using locally fetched data to refine the model further. In our tests using the all-night sleep dataset, our proposed method required roughly 30% fewer communication rounds and achieved a 94% of the accuracy compared to the original centralized approach. To support open collaboration and testing, we also release the complete codebase and simulated federated environment.

This work introduces Sparse Generative Adversarial Networks to address these issues by integrating variational autoencoder compressions with differential network competition. Specifically, the encoder maps text content into a code, which the encoder then sparsifies. In the competition phase, the generator performs fake data synthesis based on this sparse form, while the actual data helps train the classifier. The inclusion of a sparsification process aims to reduce parameter counts, enhancing model efficiency. Experimental results indicate that our method performs as effectively or better than existing approaches while achieving significantly reduced parameterization.

The scattering of multicellular organisms across planetary systems, known as panspermia, could significantly alter an system's evolutionary trajectory, potentially affecting its capacity to support complex biospheres. Although Liu and Paquette demonstrated in 1994 that atmospheric transport can move resilient multicellular organisms between stellar systems—they termed it interstellar panspermia—assessing its rates and observable signatures has remained elusive. By applying our methodology to our Sun, we determine the timescale for interstellar panspermia involving organisms with high survival thresholds. The derived estimate exceeds $10^{43}$ years, a value vastly exceeding current astrophysical limits, thereby concluding that interstellar panspermia involving such organisms does not occur around stars like the Sun.

Our findings indicate that, for a first-guess value of PPN $\gamma$, the systematic error induced resembles a parallax dependency that mirrors a widespread distortion observed by Gaia, suggesting current settings for the parameter may be responsible for part of the mission's astrometric biases. Furthermore, our work demonstrates how adjustments to the nominal PPN $\gamma$ value induce additional shifts in measured parallax data that closely mimic a specific class of residual Gaia astrometric systematics. Furthermore, our study highlights mandatory refinements both in the underlying relativistic algorithms and in associated experimental designs targeting parameters like gamma, if mission goals regarding astrometric solution precision are to be fulfilled.

This study proposes a novel open-domain QA framework called CoQANet that integrates answers drawn from the semantic fields of questions. We evaluate CoQANet against the two largest open-domain QA datasets—SQuAD 2.0 and TriviaWA. Our results demonstrate that co-answering significantly enhances system performance on both TriviaWA and SQuAD 2.0. Furthermore, we conduct in-depth analyses of prediction distributions and performance improvements to explore how leveraging commonsensical information derived from question semantics can elevate question answering outcomes. Molecular cations found in the gas phase involving oxygen and other elements are a frequent source of confusion in spectral analysis because their simulated spectra frequently exhibit significant discrepancies with observed spectra derived from laboratory experiments. Despite these challenges, few priority O-containing molecular cations suitable for further study regarding cometical spectra have been specifically identified. By systematically comparing competing theoretical calculations with high-quality laboratory data, we have flagged the class of 2-ion $(\text{HCO})_2\text{N}^{+}$ (also written as $\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}^{+}$) as particularly problematic for cometical identification due to persistent mismatches in both simulated and experimental results concerning their spectra. While current discrepancies remain unresolved, we recommend that improved computations and targeted laboratory measurements of this ion's spectra be pursued. By contrast, although laboratory spectra for the 2-ion $\text{TSN}^{+}$ (alternatively designated $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^{+}$) exhibit notable fragmentation relative to theoretical predictions, we determined through comparative analysis with spectra obtained from cometary observations that this specific ion likely exists within cometary material.

This work addresses the challenge of improving performance in homogeneous binary classification using decentralized methods. We propose novel algorithms enabling a set of independent agents, each trained on a disjoint portion of non-stationary data, to learn nearly homogeneous model parameters. Through current rounds, every agent utilizes local updates to reach consensus with others regarding these shared parameters. To ensure robustness, the proposed methods require no assumptions about the statistical distribution of data across agents other than requiring finite support, while also remaining valid for scenarios where data volumes are unbalanced.

To evaluate consistency in the resulting learned parameters relative to ideal i.i.d. training conditions, we introduce the concept of Stroll Federated Learning (SFL). For this framework, we present three distinct protocols: Stroll Asynchronous Model Exchange (SAML), Stroll Synchronous Model Exchange (SSML), and Stroll Local Update (SLU). We provide theoretical analyses specifically targeting the two explicit proposal algorithms to establish their convergence properties. A comparative evaluation of all involved methods demonstrates that the proposed walk-based approaches outperform existing state-of-the-art binary classification protocols in both the uniform and unbalanced data settings.

Individuals involved with the criminal justice system disproportionately suffer from various mental health disorders. Nevertheless, traditional policing, prosecution, and sentencing practices fail to provide adequate access to adequate mental healthcare. Drawing upon fifteen years of data from a Pennsylvania court district, this paper evaluates the mandate enforcing post-conviction access to treatment programs. Our analysis establishes that such mandatory rehabilitation improves both individual well-being and societal welfare by diminishing recidivism among offenders, alongside delivering substantial medical cost savings, with no accompanying rise in new crimes or case-related harms. Drawing on normative and experimental frameworks, we offer recommendations for implementing similar rehabilitative strategies within other regulatory frameworks.

Pixel-level annotation shortages remain a common hurdle in medical segmentation. This paper proposes integrating consistency regularization into in-exam transfer learning to address semi-supervised medical segmentation. The method introduces a novel, unique approach to enforce consistency between interpolated images and between forward and encoded/decoded processes. This technique outperformed other semi-supervised methods using only three fully labeled CT cases per study, demonstrating that even minimal annotated data can significantly enhance SOTA performance in medical segmentation when used correctly. Both fully and partially annotated datasets received comparable results with this consistent regularization strategy, supporting the hypothesis that data augmentation presents challenges during semi-supervised learning. These findings demonstrate that consistent regularization can be an effective solution for improving medical segmentation with limited annotation resources.

Given a sample $X_1, \dots, X_n$ drawn from a mixture distribution with an unknown but finite set of component distributions and unknown weights, we investigate the estimation of the average parameter $\theta^*$. This average represents a weighted combination of the individual, unaccessible parameters governing each distribution in the mixture population. Specifically, our framework extends to cases where direct sampling from the mixture is feasible, yet direct sampling from its components is not, making the estimation of these component parameters essential for determining the mean parameter $\theta^*$. Within a generalized maximum likelihood estimation approach, we demonstrate that $\theta^*$ converges consistently and achieves asymptotic normality. This average parameter is point estimated and confidence intervals are constructed with asymptotic assurance. Simulations and a practical dataset involving environmental microbe sampling are employed to validate our methodology.

Knowledge Tracing is a well-established method for modeling a student's learning process; however, most existing approaches have failed to address the efficient preprocessing, training, and accurate evaluation of interactive data streams. To bridge this gap, we introduce \textsc{pyKT}, a Python-driven toolkit designed to address current challenges in knowledge tracing. The library facilitates the management and analysis of digital educational datasets, offering robust algorithms for the processing of log-based records. \textsc{pyKT} supports a broad spectrum of contemporary Knowledge Tracing architectures, including BERT-based and graph neural network-based models. A key feature of the toolkit is its ability to generate synthetic, stream-based training data from real-world logging systems, ensuring compatibility with various training workflows while preserving the data's temporal and structural characteristics. Furthermore, \textsc{pyKT} provides the calculation of several pivotal evaluation metrics and metrics essential for validating streaming approaches. In this study, we apply the toolkit to conduct an in-depth evaluation of multiple dominant knowledge tracing models using both traditional and stream-oriented protocols. Our investigation reveals important insights into the predictive performance, computational efficiency, and operational insights derived from popular deep learning-oriented methods in tracing.

Addressing these contradictions, this paper introduces Federative Training with Buffered Asynchronous Aggregation (FedBABY). This new method operates by asynchronously updating models from participants within a secondary storage system, ensuring that training can proceed without the need to synchronize others. Ultimately, we demonstrate mathematically that convergence is still guaranteed through asynchronous aggregation, even when changes are made in an unscheduled or unrestricted manner with a high frequency of updates from participating parties.

We introduce a Temporal Difference (TD) learning strategy designed to simplify the policy learning process for marine robots navigating in linear currents. To do this, the state space valuation function is modeled as an Gaussian Process Temporal Difference (GPTD) policy. Since valuing any given state requires only a few on-orbit experiences, the method remains efficient and converges quickly. This dynamic modeling also automatically reduces the noise influence inherent in standard bootstrapping and significantly cuts off the generalization of the learned behavior beyond recently explored regions, forcing focus on where the agent has been most active. Consequently, the GPTD approach outperforms both the decimated Reynolds number and model-based planning. Testing via large-emulation simulations of a fish-like robot comparing these methods in strong linear currents shows that the GPTD strategy produces more efficient, predictable, and stable paths than either the decimated Reynolds number planning or model-based planning.

Automational speech and text systems introduce significant grammatical mistakes that require substantial post-editing efforts; although large-scale Error-Annotated (EA) datasets facilitate the creation of robust Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) models, these models typically underperform in downstream applications due to poor generalization on unlabeled data. This limitation arises further because establishing accurate annotation agreements is time-consuming and costly, resulting in EA datasets remaining relatively scarce in number. In contrast, generating vast amounts of error-containing text can be achieved easily through automated generation methods by employing existing GEC models against error-free texts. Leveraging this imbalance, we present few-shot domain transfer (FSDT) for GEC, which replaces traditional training on EA datasets with error-rich data and has the task of transferring its capabilities to a new target domain. Specifically, we utilize meta-learning to maximize the model generalization capacity using only a handful of error-annotation (EA) samples across diverse languages and domains. Experimental results spanning four languages demonstrates the effectiveness of our strategy, noting training on just one EA document can match the performance gained with typically 20 instances. Furthermore, evaluation at different amounts of source error-annotations highlights the scalability of the proposed model across multiple real-world scenarios.

The primary focus is on efficient fair allocation mechanisms that achieve Pure Nash Equilibria (PNE). A spira1 arm extends from this structure into the outer galaxy, while distinct stellar concentrations suggest former satellite interactions. Although surface brightness profiles were used initially to map the hydrodynamic disk extent alongside $21\,\rm{cm}$ CO emissions and stellar population data, a more rigorous analysis employing [NII$\,\lambda$6584]/H$\alpha$ diagnostic ratios and absolute M$_V$ corrections for the inner disk reveals an even larger, hyper-stable disk. We have executed two-current correlation function computations involving the axial and vector operators involving steps, utilizing a methodology grounded in a rigidified meson structure description. This approach enables the simultaneous calculation of numerous integrations involved in implementing the equivalent mass concept within correlation functions. Converting these functions allows us to extract the spectrum associated with states of definite quantum numbers ($J^{PC}$). For the specific case of $0^{-+}$ states corresponding to a pion, our simulation yields a mass value that aligns precisely with the physical particle expectation, confirming the method's reliability.

The regulation of protoplanetary disk evolution relies on analyzing long-term fluctuations in the accretion rates flowing onto the central star. This study examines XX Cha using 16 years of data drawn from the UV Excess Survey, complemented by numerous hours of further observations to securely determine its time-averaged accretion rate. The results reveal remarkable variability, with the mean accretion rate shifting significantly over multi-year intervals; furthermore, sudden surges in accretion were detected even over short timescales. Given that similar patterns are likely widespread among young stellar objects, this behavior must be incorporated into accuracy assessments of accretion rate distributions. Additionally, potential drivers for such variability are briefly discussed.

Multi-agent offline reinforcement learning (MARL) extracts policies from large datasets collected by multiple agents in shared environments. The effectiveness of these policies is heavily influenced by the data distribution's peak signal reward; consequently, existing research assumes access to at least one high-reward agent to serve as a seed for reinforcement learning. However, in practical settings, such a high-reward source is often unavailable, causing current methods to fail due to reward ceilings that prevent significant performance gains. We address this by proposing the Marl with Truncated Rewards (MarlTr) framework, which assumes only that some agents in the dataset possess above-average rewards rather than an extreme high-reward source. Our approach truncates negative reward signals below a specific threshold to encourage policy exploration, outperforming prior state-of-the-art algorithms on synthetic and real-world datasets. Our implementation requires no additional hyperparameter tuning and maintains a total training time comparable to existing methods with similar performance, as evidenced by experiments on both real and synthetic data environments.

We introduce a method to automate the geometric alignment of 2D/3D medical linear x-ray images, known as KBImages, which are obtained without using physical opposable scanns in the context of remote operations. We trained a single end-to-end convolutional neural network to simultaneously learn two tasks: first, to generate a 3D rendering of the scene from a set of n 2D KBImages, and second, to determine the affine transformation required to realign those n 2D KBImages. To prepare the Neural Network, we created a dataset consisting of n 2D KBImages and their matching 3D CT scans taken from the same isos, with each image manually aligned in prior step. Our model was divided into an research phase and a single transfer learning evaluation. Both the research and transfer learning steps were tested on independent datasets. During the research, we evaluated a Graph Neural Network. In the transfer learning step, we evaluated the real-world scenario. Results from the research and transfer learning steps were both considered in the analysis.

Local entanglement involving single-particle states has been confirmed through experiments utilizing interferometers that lack closed loops. However, whether such states exhibit strict nonlocality remains debatable. In this work, we demonstrate that single-particle entropy is indeed entangled in a strictly nonlocal way by showing that one-particle entropy allows for the type of steering associated with multi-particle entropy. These findings suggest that single-particle entropy is capable of producing unique forms of nonlocality that cannot be accounted for by multi-particle systems.

The integration of intelligent applications within the Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has become so essential that it is sometimes referred to as Internet of Vehicles Intelligence (IVS). However, significant challenges regarding massive mobile data collection, storage, and processing persist. Although full-scale IoVs offers opportunities, critical concerns about data privacy and security have made these technologies highly attractive yet difficult to deploy. Currently, blockchain and cloud computing represent the two primary solution paths aimed at resolving these issues. Cloud learning allows multiple users to share their mobile data for more efficient processing while maintaining individual privacy through techniques such as Federated Learning (FL). Conversely, blockchain technology offers a highly secure and trusted environment characterized by shared ledgers, strong cryptography, consensus mechanisms, and peer-to-peer architecture, capable of ensuring both the security and manageability of data in IoVS. By combining the strengths of FL and blockchain, researchers can create enhanced learning systems that offer heightened security, management efficiency, and user friendliness. This study presents a comprehensive survey of literature focusing on consensus algorithms in FL-led blockchain architectures for IoVS. Although OFDM offers robust bandwidth efficiency and resistance to noise, its susceptibility to eavesdropping hinders secure wireless communications. This study proposes a new OFDM scheme for physical layer security (PLS) that utilizes beamforming (BB) to overcome these obstacles and deliver secure, relay-assisted transmission. In this approach, a legitimate BB user (BBUs) exchanges data with an access point (BS) through an OFDM link, with assistance from cooperative relays in a way that avoids subcarrier allocation issues common to multi-tone methods. The paper formulates an optimization problem aimed at enhancing secrecy rates by jointly optimizing transmit powers and beamforming vectors. Addressing the difficulty of the non-convex objective and constraints, an iterative algorithm is developed to find satisfactory solutions. Simulation outcomes demonstrate the superiority of the suggested method when compared to conventional OFDM reception.

The feeble gravity conjecture posits that the lightest states in anti-de Sitter (AdS) space-cetimes cannot carry excessively large charges, a notion first detailed by Archibald, Puhdtsa, and Vasharshar (2020). We propose formal definitions for the related "weak and strong magnetic Swamplight conjections" within two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs). It is demonstrated, yet not limited to $\mathcal{N}=2$ symmetry that any finite number of states must satisfy the electric or magnetic versions. Furthermore, under the assumption that a certain "charged convex operator hypothesis" holds—a suggestion consistent with observed data in both rational conformal field theories and the specific large charge limits where the feeble gravity conjecture is expected to be valid—we prove the general "weak magnetic Swamlight conjecture." This specific implication suggests the strong variant may follow from the "charged convex operator hypothesis," though we have yet to establish a rigorous proof for all cases. Finally, we outline sufficient conditions ensuring the "charged convex operator hypothesis" to be satisfied in specific conformal field theory models, including those with an extensive number of conformal states that exhibit the "charged convex operator hypothesis" to be satisfied.

Although auxiliary services are integral to the operational integrity of the electricity system, current academic focus has predominantly favored the main market, often treating auxiliary services as secondary. Nevertheless, service-related policies significantly shape main market design; for instance, the integration of renewables and the evolution of market structures demand targeted auxiliary service policies, making their main market impact non-negligible. While previous concise explorations existed, most previous models omitted critical elements like the main market setting, policy parameters, and key outcomes such as market clearing prices, user utility, and operator profits. Furthermore, existing models typically ignored the interaction between primary operations and auxiliary services, and differences in acquisition mechanisms were rarely explored. Illness-aware Image Editing (IE) aims to transform healthy images into those depicting specific pathologies while preserving the inherent features of the subject. Most existing IE models based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) depend on distinct training datasets for each target object category; however, this approach is inappropriate for IE of medical conditions given their diversity and inability to separate them into clear categories. To overcome this challenge, we introduce PathologyDiff, a guidance framework that employs a disease prediction model to train a Conditioned Diffusion Model (CDM). This framework utilizes the disease score generated by the predictor as an intensity indicator to effectively instruct a diffusion model and produce images of particular illnesses from a healthy starting point. Effectiveness was validated through experiments across three distinct datasets involving an accumulated seven categories of disease. Results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art categories in multiple aspects, including image quality, clinical usability, the preservation of original eye-lane structure, and the pathological authenticity displayed by generated diseases, as assessed both quantitatively and qualitatively, with potential for broad utility in various clinical scenarios.

Vectorial data represents a set of points characterized by multiple dimensions, requiring particular techniques for storage and processing that accommodate both dimensions and values while facilitating intuitive user interaction. We present ViDaExpert, a novel software solution designed for vectorial data visualization and analysis. This tool integrates several advanced formats—including MAT, HDF5, PHANTOM, and others—with core functions for executing diverse operations such as filtering, mathematical calculations, and statistical assessments. Addressing the critical challenge of making high-dimensional data comprehensible, ViDaExpert supports techniques including Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Self-Organizing Maps (SOM), and t-Distributed Neighbor Emdding (t-SDA in context, likely t-SNE), alongside raw views such as Sphere and Slice navigation. Furthermore, the application employs integrated artificial intelligence to perform automatic classification and predicts missing values via various recursive neural networks. To validate its efficacy, we employed real-world datasets within ViDaExpert to demonstrate the practical utility of these features.
